references.title: Australian Medicines Handbook
references.locator: Benzylpenicillin and doxycycline: dosing

tutor_context: Key facts: severity is graded clinically with tools such as SMART-COP or CORB; low severity is oral amoxicillin, moderate is IV benzylpenicillin plus doxycycline or clarithromycin, high severity is ceftriaxone plus azithromycin; in tropical northern Australia and in patients with specific risks (alcohol, diabetes, Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander communities with high rates of melioidosis) regimens differ; doxycycline is avoided in pregnancy. Misconceptions: that ceftriaxone is a safe default for any admitted pneumonia; that atypical cover is optional. Out of scope: antibiotic choice in penicillin allergy and in tropical regions.
plan: Tests selection of the correct empirical regimen for moderate CAP at intern level, evidencing 4.1, 1.7 and 1.8. The Mid North evening cover with the physician by phone places the intern as prescriber. Distractors are the high-severity regimen, the low-severity oral regimen, and a hospital-acquired regimen. Supported by eTG Antibiotic and AMH.

stem: You are the junior doctor on the surgical ward of a large metropolitan teaching hospital. A 40-year-old man is day 2 after an open reduction and internal fixation of an ankle fracture and is receiving enoxaparin 40 mg daily for thromboprophylaxis. He has a history of gout, well controlled on allopurinol 300 mg daily with no flare for a year. Overnight he developed severe pain, redness and swelling of the opposite first metatarsophalangeal joint, identical to his previous flares. He is afebrile, heart rate 84/min, blood pressure 132/80 mmHg, and the surgical wound is clean. Bloods: white cell count 11.8 x 10^9/L, creatinine 128 micromol/L with eGFR 55 mL/min/1.73 m2, urate 0.48 mmol/L. The registrar asks you to sort out his gout before the round.
lead_in: Which action should you prioritise?

options.text: Cease allopurinol until the flare has settled
Continue allopurinol and start a short course of oral prednisolone
Increase allopurinol to 400 mg daily because the urate is above target
Start ibuprofen 400 mg three times daily with food

explanations.A: Stopping allopurinol during a flare is a common error; it does not shorten the flare and the fall and later rise in urate can prolong or provoke further flares. Established urate-lowering therapy is continued unchanged through a flare.
explanations.B: An acute gout flare is treated promptly with an anti-inflammatory agent while urate-lowering therapy continues. In a post-operative patient with reduced renal function and concurrent anticoagulant prophylaxis, a short course of oral prednisolone (for example 15 to 30 mg daily for 3 to 5 days) is the preferred option; low-dose colchicine is an alternative with dose adjustment for renal function. Intra-articular corticosteroid is another option if a single joint is accessible.
explanations.C: Adjusting the allopurinol dose is a decision for after the flare has resolved, and dose changes are made gradually with renal function in mind; changing it now adds nothing to the acute pain and may worsen the flare.
explanations.D: NSAIDs are effective for gout flares in otherwise well patients, but with an eGFR of 55, recent surgery and concurrent enoxaparin they carry risks of acute kidney injury and bleeding; a corticosteroid is safer here.

learning_point: Treat an acute gout flare with an anti-inflammatory agent chosen for the patient's comorbidities (corticosteroid when NSAIDs are unsuitable) and keep established allopurinol going.

references.title: Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology
references.locator: Gout: treatment of acute flares and continuation of urate-lowering therapy

references.title: Australian Medicines Handbook
references.locator: Allopurinol: practice points on continuing during flares; NSAIDs in renal impairment

tutor_context: Key facts: flare treatment options are NSAIDs, low-dose colchicine or corticosteroids, chosen by comorbidity; allopurinol is never stopped for a flare and, if newly started, is begun with flare prophylaxis; target urate is under 0.36 mmol/L (0.30 with tophi). Misconceptions: stopping or adjusting allopurinol during a flare; defaulting to NSAIDs regardless of renal function. Out of scope: septic arthritis work-up where the diagnosis is uncertain, and febuxostat.
plan: Tests the basic priority in an inpatient gout flare: treat the flare safely and leave allopurinol alone, evidencing 4.1, 1.7 and 1.8. The metropolitan surgical ward adds enoxaparin and reduced renal function to make the anti-inflammatory choice matter. Distractors are stopping allopurinol, increasing it, and an NSAID in a patient with contraindications. Supported by eTG Rheumatology and AMH.

stem: You are the junior doctor on the general ward of a metropolitan general hospital with a registrar on site. A 60-year-old man with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (ejection fraction 30%) was admitted 3 days ago with decompensation and has been receiving furosemide 80 mg intravenously twice daily alongside his usual perindopril 8 mg, bisoprolol 5 mg and spironolactone 25 mg. His weight is down 3.5 kg, he is less breathless, oxygen saturation 95% on room air, and ankle oedema has reduced but persists. This morning: heart rate 68/min, blood pressure 94/58 mmHg (124/76 on admission), creatinine 162 micromol/L (98 on admission), potassium 5.7 mmol/L (4.4 on admission), sodium 134 mmol/L. The nurse is about to give the morning doses and asks you to confirm the chart.
lead_in: Which action should take priority?

options.text: Cease furosemide and give sodium chloride 0.9% 500 mL over 30 minutes to restore the blood pressure
Increase the furosemide to 120 mg intravenously twice daily, because the ankle oedema still persists
Withhold spironolactone and perindopril, check ECG and potassium, and discuss the diuretic with the registrar
Give calcium gluconate 10% 10 mL intravenously over 5 minutes for the hyperkalaemia before the morning doses

explanations.A: He has had an effective diuresis and still has oedema; a saline bolus in a patient with a 30% ejection fraction risks pulmonary oedema. The blood pressure drop is related to volume removal plus vasodilating drugs, and stopping diuresis entirely is not the priority.
explanations.B: Increasing the diuretic when creatinine has risen 60% and blood pressure has fallen would worsen the kidney injury and hypotension; the diuretic needs review, not escalation.
explanations.C: A rising creatinine, potassium of 5.7 mmol/L and falling blood pressure in a patient on an ACE inhibitor and a mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist during aggressive diuresis signal that these drugs must be paused today. The junior doctor should withhold the potassium-retaining and blood-pressure-lowering agents before the doses are given, check an ECG for hyperkalaemic changes, repeat the potassium, and involve the registrar in deciding whether the diuretic is reduced or held. This prevents a preventable adverse drug event and sits squarely within a junior doctor's responsibility for the chart.
explanations.D: Calcium gluconate is for hyperkalaemia with ECG changes or potassium of 6.5 mmol/L or more; at 5.7 mmol/L with no ECG yet, the priority is to stop the drugs driving it and measure, not to give calcium.

learning_point: During diuresis in heart failure, a rise in creatinine with hyperkalaemia and hypotension means withholding the ACE inhibitor or ARB and mineralocorticoid antagonist that morning, checking an ECG and potassium, and reviewing the diuretic with a senior before more doses are given.

references.title: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular
references.locator: Heart failure: monitoring renal function and potassium with ACE inhibitors and mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists

references.title: National Heart Foundation of Australia and Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand, Guidelines for the prevention, detection and management of heart failure in Australia 2018
references.locator: Management of acute decompensated heart failure; dose adjustment of RAAS inhibitors with renal dysfunction and hyperkalaemia

references.title: Australian Medicines Handbook
references.locator: Spironolactone: hyperkalaemia precautions; ACE inhibitors: renal impairment

tutor_context: Key facts: spironolactone is withheld for potassium above 5.5 mmol/L or a marked creatinine rise; ACE inhibitors are paused for symptomatic hypotension or acute kidney injury; a small creatinine rise during diuresis is expected but a 50% or greater rise with hyperkalaemia needs action; the beta blocker is usually continued unless bradycardic or shocked. Misconceptions: that oedema means the diuretic must increase; that fluid should be given for any hypotension. Out of scope: inotropes and ultrafiltration.

The metropolitan ward with a registrar on site makes early discussion realistic. Distractors are saline, more diuretic and calcium. Supported by eTG Cardiovascular, the NHFA/CSANZ heart failure guideline and AMH.

stem: You are the junior doctor in the emergency department of a tertiary hospital in Adelaide. A 38-year-old man is brought in by ambulance with 2 weeks of worsening breathlessness, orthopnoea and leg swelling after a flu-like illness a month ago, now acutely worse over 2 hours. He is sitting forward, sweaty, speaking in single words. Respiratory rate 32/min, oxygen saturation 86% on 8 L/min via Hudson mask, heart rate 124/min regular, blood pressure 158/96 mmHg, temperature 37.2 C. Widespread crackles to the mid-zones and a raised jugular venous pressure. The ECG shows sinus tachycardia with left bundle branch block of unknown age. Venous gas: pH 7.29, PaCO2 52 mmHg, lactate 2.8 mmol/L. A chest X-ray is being done at the bedside. The emergency consultant is in the next bay and has said to call when you have assessed him.
lead_in: Which action should you prioritise first?

options.text: Give furosemide 40 mg intravenously and insert a urinary catheter to monitor the diuretic response
Send troponin, B-type natriuretic peptide and blood cultures and await the results before treatment
Request an urgent bedside echocardiogram to define the cause of heart failure before starting treatment
Sit him upright, give sublingual glyceryl trinitrate 400 micrograms and call the consultant now to start CPAP

explanations.A: Intravenous diuretic is part of treatment for acute pulmonary oedema with fluid overload, but it acts over 30 to 60 minutes and does not address the immediate respiratory failure; it follows the airway and breathing steps and the nitrate.
explanations.B: These tests are needed for diagnosis and will be sent, but waiting on results in a patient with hypoxaemia, rising carbon dioxide and acidosis is unsafe; treatment comes first.
explanations.C: An echocardiogram will define the likely dilated cardiomyopathy after a viral illness, but it does not change the first-hour resuscitation and should not delay respiratory support.
explanations.D: This is acute cardiogenic pulmonary oedema with hypercapnic respiratory failure in a young man with probable new cardiomyopathy. The priorities are positioning, non-invasive ventilation (CPAP reduces work of breathing, improves oxygenation and reduces preload and afterload, and is recommended for pulmonary oedema with respiratory distress or acidosis), and nitrate vasodilation while blood pressure is adequate, with immediate senior involvement because he may need intubation or intensive care. Diuretic, investigations and echocardiography follow.

learning_point: In acute pulmonary oedema with respiratory distress or acidosis, the first priorities are upright positioning, nitrate if blood pressure allows, non-invasive ventilation and immediate senior help; diuretics and investigations come next.
setting_note: In a regional hospital without on-site ICU, the same first steps apply with whatever non-invasive support is available, and the retrieval service should be called at the same time because this patient may need intubation and transfer.

references.title: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular
references.locator: Acute heart failure and pulmonary oedema: initial management, nitrates and non-invasive ventilation

references.title: National Heart Foundation of Australia and Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand, Guidelines for the prevention, detection and management of heart failure in Australia 2018
references.locator: Acute heart failure: non-invasive ventilation, vasodilators and diuretics

tutor_context: Key facts: in acute pulmonary oedema with hypertension or normal blood pressure, nitrates and CPAP or bilevel ventilation are first-line with diuretics for volume overload; hypotension or shock changes the approach to inotropes and senior or ICU care; opioids are no longer routine. Misconceptions: that furosemide is the first drug in all pulmonary oedema; that investigations must precede treatment. Out of scope: inotrope selection and mechanical support.

The tertiary emergency department has CPAP and a consultant nearby. Distractors are the reflex diuretic, waiting on bloods and imaging. Supported by eTG Cardiovascular and the NHFA/CSANZ heart failure guideline.

stem: You are the intern on the general medicine team at a tertiary hospital in Adelaide, which provides a daily telehealth ward round to a regional hospital's medical ward. On today's video call the regional nurse presents a 56-year-old woman admitted 2 days ago with a community-acquired pneumonia, who has type 2 diabetes managed with metformin and gliclazide at home and is now on prednisolone 50 mg daily for coexisting asthma. Her capillary blood glucose readings over the past 24 hours have been 13 to 19 mmol/L, highest in the late afternoon. She is eating about half her meals, has no ketones on a point-of-care test, and her creatinine is normal. The regional hospital uses a subcutaneous insulin chart that requires the treating team to document a blood glucose target range before supplemental insulin can be prescribed. The nurse asks what target range your team wants documented.
lead_in: Which blood glucose target range is recommended for this hospital inpatient?

options.text: 5 to 10 mmol/L
4 to 7 mmol/L
8 to 15 mmol/L
Below 20 mmol/L

explanations.A: Australian Diabetes Society guidance for most non-critically ill hospital inpatients recommends a blood glucose target of 5 to 10 mmol/L, balancing avoidance of hyperglycaemia (infection risk, dehydration, poor wound healing) against the harm of inpatient hypoglycaemia. Her corticosteroid-induced pattern will need a morning intermediate-acting or basal insulin plus supplemental doses, which the registrar can direct once the target is set.
explanations.B: A target of 4 to 7 mmol/L is a tight outpatient fasting target in selected patients; in hospital it increases the risk of hypoglycaemia, particularly in a patient eating unpredictably, and is not recommended.
explanations.C: An upper limit of 15 mmol/L is too permissive; sustained readings above 10 mmol/L are associated with worse outcomes in acute illness and should prompt adjustment of therapy.
explanations.D: Simply avoiding readings above 20 mmol/L is not a treatment target; it would leave her persistently hyperglycaemic and is a trigger for urgent review, not a goal.

learning_point: For most non-critically ill hospital inpatients with diabetes the recommended blood glucose target range is 5 to 10 mmol/L.
setting_note: On a telehealth ward round the target and insulin plan must be documented clearly in the regional hospital's chart, with explicit instructions on what glucose readings should prompt the nurse to phone the team, since no doctor from the team is physically present.

references.title: Australian Diabetes Society, Guidelines for routine glucose control in hospital
references.locator: Recommended blood glucose targets for non-critically ill inpatients (5 to 10 mmol/L)

references.title: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology
references.locator: Managing diabetes in hospital: glycaemic targets and glucocorticoid-induced hyperglycaemia

tutor_context: Key facts: inpatient target 5 to 10 mmol/L for most patients, somewhat higher for frail patients at risk of hypoglycaemia; sliding-scale insulin alone is discouraged; glucocorticoid hyperglycaemia peaks in the afternoon and evening and is managed with morning intermediate-acting insulin; sulfonylureas are often withheld when intake is poor. Misconceptions: that outpatient HbA1c-based targets apply in hospital; that readings under 15 are acceptable. Out of scope: insulin dose calculation and management of ketosis.

The telehealth ward round from Adelaide makes the documented target the practical link between the team and the regional nurse. Distractors are a tight outpatient target and two over-permissive ranges. Supported by the ADS inpatient guideline and eTG Endocrinology.

stem: You are the PGY2 in the emergency department of a regional hospital with no ICU, on-site CT during business hours only and retrieval to Adelaide by road or air. A 79-year-old man presents at 19:00 with a sprained ankle after a fall from a step. The triage nurse is concerned because his blood pressure is 198/108 mmHg, confirmed on three readings 10 minutes apart in both arms. He tells you he ran out of amlodipine 2 weeks ago. He has no headache, visual disturbance, chest pain, breathlessness or neurological symptoms, and is fully orientated. Heart rate 76/min, saturation 97% on room air. Examination: no focal neurology, chest clear, no new murmur; fundoscopy shows arteriolar narrowing without haemorrhages or papilloedema. ECG shows sinus rhythm with voltage criteria for left ventricular hypertrophy and no acute change. Creatinine 92 micromol/L (baseline 90), urinalysis trace protein, no blood. The ankle X-ray is normal.
lead_in: Which interpretation of his blood pressure is most accurate?

options.text: Hypertensive emergency requiring intravenous labetalol and retrieval to Adelaide tonight for monitoring
Severe hypertension without acute target organ damage, managed with oral therapy and GP review within days
Pain-related blood pressure elevation needing analgesia only and no antihypertensive action
Probable secondary hypertension requiring urgent renal artery imaging before discharge

explanations.A: A hypertensive emergency is defined by acute target organ damage (encephalopathy, retinal haemorrhages or papilloedema, acute pulmonary oedema, acute coronary syndrome, aortic dissection, acute kidney injury or stroke), not by the number alone. He has none, and acute intravenous lowering in a 79-year-old with chronic hypertension risks hypoperfusion of brain and kidneys.
explanations.B: Blood pressure of 180/110 mmHg or more without evidence of acute target organ damage is severe (sometimes called asymptomatic severe) hypertension. Australian guidance is to resume or start oral antihypertensive therapy, avoid rapid reduction, and arrange review within days to confirm control, with safety-net advice about symptoms that would prompt return. Restarting his amlodipine tonight and ensuring supply and GP follow-up is the appropriate plan.
explanations.C: Pain and anxiety can raise blood pressure, but readings this high that persist across three measurements in a man who has stopped his antihypertensive are not explained by a mild ankle sprain, and leaving him untreated with no follow-up would be unsafe.
explanations.D: Secondary causes are considered in resistant or early-onset hypertension or with suggestive features; here the obvious cause is cessation of treatment, and renal artery imaging is neither urgent nor available overnight.

learning_point: Severe hypertension is classified by the presence or absence of acute target organ damage, not the reading alone; without such damage it is managed with oral therapy and early outpatient review, not intravenous drugs.
setting_note: In a regional emergency department the key rural decision is recognising which patients need retrieval: those with acute target organ damage do, while a patient with asymptomatic severe hypertension can be discharged home with medication, a confirmed supply and a GP appointment within a few days.

tutor_context: Key facts: hypertensive emergency equals severe hypertension with acute target organ damage and needs controlled intravenous lowering in a monitored setting; asymptomatic severe hypertension is managed orally with follow-up in days; rapid lowering in chronic hypertension risks stroke and renal hypoperfusion; check fundi, neurology, ECG, creatinine and urinalysis. Misconceptions: treating the number; labelling all readings above 180/110 as emergencies. Out of scope: choice of intravenous agent in true emergencies and aortic dissection targets.
plan: Tests interpretation of a very high reading without target organ damage as asymptomatic severe hypertension rather than an emergency, evidencing 4.1, 1.7 and 1.4. The regional emergency department makes the retrieval-versus-discharge distinction concrete. Distractors are the emergency label, dismissal as pain, and premature secondary work-up.
